cf.title: Add ASCII fast path to Unicode normalization functions

input.subject: Add ASCII fast path to Unicode normalization functions

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The problem and the workload are stated (`url IS NORMALIZED` over ClickBench data), the change adds no user-visible surface, and message #3 measured no regression on non-ASCII input. The patch reuses the existing is_valid_ascii() and stays inside varlena.c. Confidence is medium because the code was not read and no benchmark of v5 as a whole is shown.

brief.title: ASCII fast path for Unicode normalization functions
brief.problem: unicode_is_normalized(), unicode_assigned() and normalize() decode every input to char32_t code points before doing any work, even when the input is pure ASCII. This makes queries like `url IS NORMALIZED` over mostly-ASCII data slow. The author cites a LinkedIn post reporting a 6x gap to CedarDB at a matched thread count.
brief.proposed_design: A SIMD byte scan with the existing is_valid_ascii() finds the leading valid ASCII prefix, and an all-ASCII string returns at once. Otherwise only the rest is decoded, starting with the last ASCII character so it can still compose with a following combining mark. unicode_assigned() walks the rest without counting code points first, and the form argument is matched in the text value without building a C string.
author_claims: About 10x faster on pure ASCII and about 4x on an 85/15 ASCII/non-ASCII mix, with no measurable regression on non-ASCII input.
ASCII has no decomposition, a combining class of zero, and is fully assigned, so results stay the same in all four forms.
Restarting at the last ASCII character gives the same quick-check answer as starting from the beginning of the string.
Allocating the C string for the form name is a noticeable part of the cost once the fast path is taken.
brief.thread_state: Chao Li, Tristan Partin, David Wheeler and Rui Zhao replied in favour, and Bilal and Rui contributed code that v5 folds in. Tristan's last comment nits remain, and Andrew plans to commit during the November CF and fix them then.
unclear: The material gives no benchmark of v5 as a whole against master.
The thread does not show results on platforms without SIMD support for is_valid_ascii(), or on big-endian machines.
The material does not say whether the first message's numbers come from the same machine and data as later runs.
Matching the form name in the text value claims to keep case-insensitive matching, but the material does not show how this handles non-ASCII or locale-dependent case.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: varlena.c gains an ASCII-prefix path and hand-written form-name matching that must stay in agreement with the full decode path.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Every call to normalize(), IS NORMALIZED and unicode_assigned() now runs a byte scan first, including on non-ASCII input.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: What does v5 as a whole measure against master on all-ASCII, mixed, non-ASCII and late-non-ASCII input?
What do the non-ASCII and late-non-ASCII cases measure on a build where is_valid_ascii() has no SIMD support?
Does an invalid form name still raise the same error when the input string is all ASCII?
Does the form-name matching in the text value accept and reject exactly the same names as the old pg_strcasecmp() path, including non-ASCII bytes in the name?
Has the patch been run on a big-endian machine?

committability.owner_note: Andrew Dunstan wrote the patch and, per the thread state, plans to commit it during the November CommitFest.
committability.liability: The owner signs for identical results in all four normalization forms, because expression indexes and CHECK constraints on normalize() or IS NORMALIZED depend on them. The liability lasts as long as the fast path exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author folded Bilal's and Rui's code into v5 and plans to fix Tristan's remaining comment nits at commit.

priority.reason: Users who run normalize() or IS NORMALIZED over mostly-ASCII text gain about 10 times on pure ASCII per message #1, confirmed in message #3. The patch is 18.4 KB in one backend file plus regression tests, and adds no user-visible surface.

provisional_note: Without the code, I could not check that restarting at the last ASCII character gives the same result as a full decode, or that form-name matching and its error behaviour match the old path. Builds without SIMD support and big-endian machines are untested in the material.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: CREATE DATABASE ... STRICT_UNICODE
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a per-database option STRICT_UNICODE that rejects text containing Unicode code points that are unassigned in the Unicode version Postgres is built with. It builds on the committed unicode_assigned() function and aims to make normalization stable and to reduce the risk of collation changes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer took up the STRICT_UNICODE patch. The author said the CF app did not point at the latest patch, agreed to move it to the next release, and later withdrew it for lack of interest. The visible messages show no objection to the per-database option itself.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I'm withdrawing this patch due to lack of interest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert COPY OUT to follow the pre-8.3 handling of ASCII control characters, namely that \r, \n, \t, \b, \f, \v are dumped as those two-character...
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert COPY OUT to follow the pre-8.3 handling of ASCII control characters, namely that \r, \n, \t, \b, \f, \v are dumped as those two-character representations rather than a backslash and the literal control character. I had made it do the other to save some code, but this was ill-advised, because dump files in which these characters appear literally are prone to newline mangling.  Fortunately, doing it the old way should only cost a few more lines of code, and not slow down the copy loop materially. Per bug #3795 from Lou Duchez.

This reverts commit eb0d0d2c7300c9c5c22b35975c11265aa4becc84.

After I had committed eb0d0d2c7 and 78ab944cd, I decided to add

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_upgrade check for Unicode update
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Robert Haas, Joe Conway, Nathan Bossart
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a pg_upgrade check that detects a change in the Unicode version between the old and new clusters. When the version changes, pg_upgrade warns and writes a list of relations that may be affected, such as indexes using the builtin provider, to a file.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No message states the withdrawal, but the last messages show reviewers favoring another approach. Robert Haas and Joe Conway argued that stability needs support for old Unicode versions alongside new ones, and Jeff Davis answered with a plan for versioned collation and ctype providers. Nathan Bossart asked whether a warning is enough and what users should do with the list of relations.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The way to actually provide the stability that people want here is to continue supporting old versions while adding support for new versions.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix pg_stat_statements display of normalized FETCH counts
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a query_normalized flag to pgssEntry, so a FETCH with a count can replace an unnormalized query text stored earlier by a FETCH without a count. A new pgss_store() parameter limits this replacement to FETCH, because SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION would break otherwise.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier said the expectation was wrong: both FETCH forms jumble to the same node once howMany is ignored, and pg_stat_statements keeps the first query string it sees. He also rejected the extra generate_normalized_query() call because it makes pg_stat_statements heavier. He named a new FetchDirectionKeywords value in gram.y as the right fix if the two forms ever need to be told apart, but saw no monitoring gain. The author then withdrew the patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: PGSERVICEFILE as part of a normal connection string [duplicated please delete]
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a libpq connection parameter "servicefile", so a connection string can name the service file directly; until now only the PGSERVICEFILE environment variable could. The parameter takes priority over PGSERVICEFILE, and a "servicefile" key inside a service file is an error.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No one objected to the idea. The entry title marks it as a duplicate commitfest entry to delete, and it was withdrawn on the day Ryo Kanbayashi posted a reworked patch set. Earlier, Michael Paquier returned the original patch with feedback because the author did not answer his review, which asked for split patches, tests for the existing service features and Windows line-ending handling.

precedents_retrieved.title: URL extension with Unicode and setter-functions support
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Daniel Gustafsson, Robert Haas, Matthias van de Meent
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a url data type as a contrib extension that parses URLs per the WHATWG URL living standard and provides functions to get and set individual URL parts. The patch reused the author's own lexbor parser code in a non-Postgres style and used ICU for Unicode TR46 host processing.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers held that a URL type belongs in an external extension, because no reason was given to ship it in core and people disagree on how URLs should be parsed. Shipping one implementation would privilege it over others. Other objections were that parsing implementations disagree on unusual URLs, that normalization means stored URLs do not come back as written, and that a living standard can change under a stable contrib release.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
For something that's part of
PostgreSQL itself, it's a big problem. There's no reason that we
should privilege one implementation over others, and we certainly do
not want the core project to have to maintain and ship multiple
versions of things like this.

precedents_retrieved.title: PgVA aka PostgresVectorAcceleration using SIMD vector instructions starting with hex_encode
precedents_retrieved.summary: Hans Buschmann proposed a SIMD acceleration framework for Postgres, starting with hex_encode, using leaf loops in NASM assembly tuned for AVX512 with AVX2/SSE2 fallbacks. A dispatcher picks the implementation from CPU capabilities, and a GUC can turn it off.
precedents_retrieved.objection: John Naylor objected to the design: NASM assembly makes the project handle object formats and calling conventions per OS, AVX512 is fragmented and missing on some Intel server hardware, and a GUC is the wrong way to choose a hardware implementation. He also rejected trading code style for speed, said the benchmark did not show patched versus unpatched results, and suggested starting with a simple SSE2 intrinsics patch. The visible messages show no revised patch after this review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: As I implied earlier, this is way too low-level. If we have to worry about obj formats and calling conventions, we'd better be getting something *really* amazing in return.

precedents_retrieved.title: optimize several list functions with SIMD intrinsics
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch uses SIMD intrinsics to speed up the linear searches in several List functions, such as list_member_int, list_member_ptr and list_delete_int, on x86 and Arm. It follows the approach used earlier for XidInMVCCSnapshot and shows about 2 times faster searches in a microbenchmark.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No workload was shown where these List functions matter, and the author agreed that a profile showing them should come first. Heikki Linnakangas checked callers such as tlist_member and list_delete_ptr, found none in hot code paths where the change would make a noticeable difference, and returned the patch with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Grepping for "tlist_member" and "list_delete_ptr", I don't see any
callers in hot codepaths where this could make a noticeable difference.

precedents_retrieved.title: Unicode mapping scripts cleanup
precedents_retrieved.summary: A series of patches cleans up the Unicode mapping scripts in src/backend/utils/mb/Unicode/ by fixing wrong comments, missing makefile pieces and similar problems. The goal is to get the scripts working again, so that changes to the CJK mappings could be considered later.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund marked the entry returned with feedback because the thread had made little progress, even though he called the patches generally a good idea. Most of the discussion was about whether to change existing mappings, which Tatsuo Ishii said would break user applications. The author had said he was not proposing to change the mappings.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I've marked this as returned-with-feedback for now, since there hasn't
been much progress lately.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
precedents_retrieved.authors: Michael Paquier, Alexander Korotkov, Simon Riggs
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
Reverted commit(s): Fix handling of orphaned 2PC files in the future at recovery; Fix failures with incorrect epoch handling for 2PC files at recovery; Make use FullTransactionId in 2PC filenames; Speedup 2PC recovery by skipping two phase state files in normal path
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 8f67f994e8ea (down to v13) and c3de0f9eed38 (down to
v17), as these are proving to not be completely correct regarding two
aspects:
- In v17 and newer branches, c3de0f9eed38's check for epoch handling is
incorrect, and does not correctly handle frozen epochs.  A logic closer
to widen_snapshot_xid() should be used.  The 2PC code should try to
integrate deeper with FullTransactionIds, 5a1dfde8334b being not enough.
- In v13 and newer branches, 8f67f994e8ea is a workaround for the real
issue, which is that we should not attempt CLOG lookups without reaching
consistency.  This exists since 728bd991c3c4, and this is reachable with
ProcessTwoPhaseBuffer() called by restoreTwoPhaseData() at the beginning
of recovery.

Per discussion with Noah Misch.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P9] (SIMD for List functions) shares only the SIMD keyword, and its reason does not apply: it stalled because no hot workload was shown, while this proposal names one (url IS NORMALIZED on ClickBench) and three reviewers measured it. The thread points to no earlier attempt at this idea.

The patch changes no SQL syntax, function signature, GUC, catalog or dump output, and the stated results of normalize(), IS NORMALIZED and unicode_assigned() stay the same in all four forms. The one possible contract change is form-name matching done in the text value, and v5 adds regression tests for invalid and mixed-case form names. Two points cannot be checked without the code: whether an invalid form still raises an error for all-ASCII input, and whether case folding still matches pg_strcasecmp().

The patch changes only src/backend/utils/adt/varlena.c and regression files, with no catalog, WAL, on-disk, wire protocol or exported header change. The one persistent link is expression indexes and CHECK constraints built on normalize() or IS NORMALIZED, which would need reindexing after pg_upgrade if results changed, but the proposal claims identical results in all four forms and tests prefix sweeps, so no failure scenario stands.

The proposal changes only how three existing SQL functions compute their results, so it has no privilege or exposure aspect. It adds no object, privilege, setting or new input path, and the results for every input stay the same, so non-superusers gain nothing new. Rejecting invalid form names is a correctness question for the code review.

From the maintenance and fit angle I find no objection a committer would send. The change stays inside varlena.c and its regression tests, adds no GUC, catalog, ABI or dependency, and reuses the existing is_valid_ascii(). Its correctness rests on ASCII having no decomposition, being all starters and being fully assigned, and Unicode stability rules keep those facts fixed. On the hot path, non-ASCII input pays one byte scan, and message #3 and message #5 measured no regression there and a gain on late non-ASCII input. The author is a committer who plans to commit and own it, and four other people reviewed or contributed. [P9] does not fit: it was returned because no workload used the List functions, while this patch targets `IS NORMALIZED` and normalize() on real text columns. The material does not show runs on builds without SIMD support or on big-endian machines, and checking that the form-name matching agrees with the old parsing needs the code.

No existing feature, extension or hook gives the same result. Users could precheck with a regex or an encoding test before calling normalize(), but that only moves the same work into SQL and does not speed up the built-in functions. The patch reuses the existing is_valid_ascii() and adds no new mechanism, so item 12 is not at issue. [P9] does not fit, because this thread shows a concrete workload (IS NORMALIZED over ClickBench URLs).

The thread shows enough demand for an internal speedup that adds no user-visible surface. Two people wrote the same patch independently after one public benchmark (messages #1, #7), four others reviewed or added code, and the target workload is named: `url IS NORMALIZED` over ClickBench data. The cost stays inside varlena.c and falls only on callers of these functions. Message #3 shows no regression on non-ASCII input. [P9] does not apply, because it failed for lack of any workload and this proposal names one.
